name: Worker monitoring combined with communications isolation

attribution.legal_posture: Source-attributed qualitative interview evidence; legal finding, workforce-wide prevalence, identity, nationality, and misconduct status require separate evidence.

caveats: Monitoring, communications behavior, quota pressure, subcontracting, trading activity, geography, language, and any single signal require corroboration before supporting identity, nationality, sanctions, or misconduct attribution.
Evidence and method class: source-attributed qualitative interviews with a small number of former IT workers or IT experts.
Fraudulent employment, general DPRK overseas labor, sanctions evasion, and malicious cyber activity remain analytically distinct unless a cited source expressly connects them.

Publish only as review-level, source-attributed labor-control context. Monitoring software, communications patterns, and isolation are contextual; applicant-screening and nationality indicators require job-relevant corroboration.
Some participant names are pseudonyms; actor attribution requires corroboration.
The report contains 15 interviews overall, with a small subset described as former IT workers or IT experts; it supplies a non-representative IT-worker sample.
The report leaves prevalence of the described monitoring software across organizations, countries, and time periods unreported.
This record is policy, labor-governance, economic, or sanctions-evasion context; person, organization, victim, account, transaction, and incident profiles require separate records.

infrastructure.evidence_method_class: source-attributed qualitative interviews with a small number of former IT workers or IT experts
infrastructure.statement: PSCORE interviewees described supervisors using screen-monitoring software, reprimanding workers who disabled it, and restricting both in-person and online communications. This adds a labor-governance dimension to monitoring already represented as a production-control TTP: the same controls can enforce isolation and constrain worker autonomy, not merely measure output.
sampling_limitations: The report contains 15 interviews overall, but only a small subset is described as former IT workers or IT experts; it does not provide a representative IT-worker sample.
The report does not establish the prevalence of the described monitoring software across organizations, countries, or time periods.
Some participant names are pseudonyms and are not suitable for actor attribution.
